entities.name: Marcus Petreius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Petreius, a Roman general and politician born in Picenum, distinguished himself as a steadfast military commander and a loyal client of Pompey the Great during the tumultuous final decades of the Roman Republic, ultimately dying by suicide in 45 BCE. His career is intrinsically linked to the violent political upheavals of his era, most notably his decisive role in crushing the Catilinarian Conspiracy and his unwavering support for the Optimates during Caesar's Civil War. Petreius represents a type of Roman military professional whose competence and allegiance were forged in an age of escalating internal conflict, making him a critical, if secondary, figure in the transition from Republic to Empire.

Petreius's military prowess first gained prominence during the Sertorian War in Hispania (76–72 BCE), where he served as a legate under Pompey. His most celebrated achievement, however, came on the fields outside Pistoia in 62 BCE. Acting as the senior legate under the consul Gaius Antonius Hybrida, Petreius effectively commanded the consular legions against the rebel forces of Lucius Sergius Catilina. Demonstrating tactical acumen, Petreius cornered Catiline's desperate army, leading the charge personally and ensuring the utter annihilation of the conspiracy, with Catiline himself falling in battle. This victory preserved the Roman state from a serious internal threat and solidified Petreius's reputation as a reliable and formidable general.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Marcus Petreius played a crucial role in ending the Catilinarian Conspiracy, a major internal threat to the Roman Republic, and was a prominent general for the Pompeian faction throughout Caesar's Civil War, influencing the duration and intensity of the conflict.
